meta.title: Caught-In/Between Hazards in Construction Environments
meta.description: Covers recognition, prevention, and control of caught-in/between hazards on construction sites, including trench cave-ins, unguarded machinery, equipment pinch zones, scaffold instability, and demolition collapse.

caught-in-between-overview.title: Understanding Caught-In/Between Hazards
caught-in-between-overview.content:
Caught-in/between hazards occur when a worker is caught, crushed, squeezed, pinned, or compressed between objects, materials, equipment, machinery, trenches, or collapsing structures. OSHA includes caught-in/between among the 'Top Four' construction fatality hazard categories, alongside falls, struck-by hazards, and electrocutions.

Key characteristics:
- Can occur with moving equipment or between a moving and fixed object
- May involve trenches, machinery, tools, vehicles, equipment rollovers, loads, formwork, or collapsing structures
- Often develop quickly — a machine starts, soil shifts, a load swings, or a vehicle backs up
- Differ from struck-by hazards: struck-by involves contact from a moving object; caught-in/between involves trapping, crushing, or compression

Recognize the key terms: pinch point, crush zone, nip point, swing radius, collapse zone, and entanglement hazard.

jobsite-hazard-recognition.title: Jobsite Hazard Recognition
jobsite-hazard-recognition.content:
Before and during any task, workers must actively scan the work area for caught-in/between hazards.

What to look for:
- Moving equipment, tight clearances, unstable materials, suspended loads
- Unguarded machine parts, trenches, scaffold changes, demolition activities
- Changing ground conditions, especially after rain or nearby traffic

Questions to ask before starting work:
- What can move, collapse, roll, rotate, shift, swing, or trap me?
- Are there equipment blind spots or swing radii nearby?
- Are protective systems, guards, barriers, and spotters in place?

Common examples of recognized hazards: walking behind a skid-steer without eye contact with the operator, stacked masonry block near walkways, or working next to a trench after rainfall without reassessment.

tools-machinery-guards.title: Tools, Machinery, Guards, and Moving Parts
tools-machinery-guards.content:
Entanglement and crushing hazards from tools and machinery are a major caught-in/between concern.

OSHA 1926.300 requires:
- Tools to be maintained in safe condition
- Guards on power-operated tools when designed for guarding
- Moving parts such as belts, gears, shafts, pulleys, sprockets, drums, chains, and similar components must be guarded when exposed to employee contact

Safe practices:
- Never remove or bypass guards
- Keep hands, clothing, jewelry, gloves, and cords away from moving parts
- Use the right tool for the job
- Remove defective tools from service immediately
- Shut down and control energy before clearing jams, changing blades, or making adjustments

Remember: a guard is not an inconvenience — it is a barrier between you and an injury that can happen faster than you can react.

excavations-trenches-cave-ins.title: Excavations, Trenches, and Cave-In Prevention
excavations-trenches-cave-ins.content:
Being trapped or crushed in a trench cave-in is one of the most severe caught-in/between hazards. OSHA's excavation standards are in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P.

Key rule: Never enter an unprotected trench or excavation that requires a protective system.

Approved protective methods:
- Sloping: cutting back the trench wall at an angle
- Benching: creating horizontal steps in the trench wall
- Shoring: installing supports to prevent collapse
- Shielding: using a trench box to protect workers

Hazard triggers that require reassessment:
- Water accumulation
- Cracks, vibrations, or ground shifting
- Surcharge loads (nearby equipment, spoil piles)
- Traffic near the excavation
- Rain or changing weather conditions

Soil can look stable right up until it fails. Appearance is not protection — a protective system is protection.

vehicles-heavy-equipment.title: Vehicles, Heavy Equipment, and Pinch Zones
vehicles-heavy-equipment.content:
Dump trucks, skid-steers, excavators, forklifts, loaders, compactors, cranes, and other mobile equipment create pinch zone and crushing hazards.

Core rules:
- Stay out of blind spots and swing radii at all times
- Never position yourself between moving equipment and a fixed object
- Establish traffic control, spotter communication, backup procedures, barricades, and exclusion zones
- Do not ride on equipment unless it is designed for passengers

If you cannot see the operator, the operator may not see you. Never assume equipment will stop before you are pinned.

OSHA coverage:
- Subpart O (1926.600) — Motor vehicles and mechanized equipment
- 1926.1400 (Subpart CC) — Cranes and derricks; all workers must stay clear of swing radii and load paths

Communication tools: hand signals, spotters, radio, exclusion zone markings, and pre-task planning.

scaffolds-structural-instability.title: Scaffolds, Concrete/Masonry, and Structural Instability
scaffolds-structural-instability.content:
Unstable scaffolds, collapsing formwork, shifting precast members, masonry wall instability, and structural loads create caught-in/between risks.

Scaffold hazards (1926 Subpart L / 1926.451):
- Scaffolds must be properly designed, erected, supported, loaded, and inspected
- Never move a scaffold while materials remain unsecured
- Load limits must not be exceeded

Concrete and masonry hazards (1926 Subpart Q):
- Formwork and shores can fail if removed before concrete achieves adequate strength
- Masonry walls require adequate bracing during construction
- Precast panels can shift during placement
- Limited access zones must be established near masonry wall construction

Key principle: many caught-in/between hazards involve stored energy — weight, pressure, tension, gravity, or movement. If a structure or load shifts, you do not want your body in the path.

demolition-collapse-zones.title: Demolition, Collapse Zones, and Changing Conditions
demolition-collapse-zones.content:
Demolition, renovation, and dismantling operations create dynamic caught-in/between risks as structural support changes with each element removed.

OSHA 1926.850 (Demolition: Preparatory Operations) requires:
- A competent person to perform an engineering survey before demolition begins
- Written evidence of the engineering survey
- Shoring or bracing of damaged or weakened structures
- Control of all utilities (electrical, gas, water, sewer) before demolition starts

Safe demolition practices:
- Plan the sequence of demolition with an engineer
- Shore or brace walls and floors before removing supports
- Establish barricades and drop zones for debris
- Reassess conditions continuously as materials are removed
- Keep unauthorized workers out of collapse zones

Demolition hazards are rarely static. As material is removed, loads shift and support changes. A safe area in the morning may not be safe in the afternoon.

prevention-communication.title: Prevention, Communication, and Reporting
prevention-communication.content:
Daily prevention practices and open communication are essential to eliminating caught-in/between injuries.

Pre-task controls:
- Pre-task hazard review and job hazard analysis (JHA)
- Toolbox talks focused on site-specific conditions
- Competent person inspections for excavations, scaffolds, and demolition
- Spotters, lockout procedures, barriers, and warning signs
- Stop-work authority for all workers

What to report:
- Near misses — any situation where someone could have been trapped or crushed
- Missing or damaged equipment guards
- Unprotected trenches or changed soil conditions
- Unstable materials, unsecured loads, or shifting structures
- Unsafe equipment positioning or backing procedures

A near miss is a warning. Reporting it gives the crew a chance to fix the condition before someone is trapped, crushed, or buried. All workers have the right and responsibility to stop work when a hazard is identified.
